source_review.notes: Reviewed current ISO C++ unordered-container requirements, Java SE 25 HashMap documentation, OpenJDK HashMap source, Redis dict.h/dict.c, Linux hlist documentation, Rust HashMap, and Abseil Swiss Tables, plus the primary Carter-Wegman and Crosby-Wallach papers. All ten final destinations returned HTTP 200. OpenJDK and Redis private details are explicitly source/version scoped.

evidence: Checked T/Bi/Li/m/n/alpha/Lmax, full-hash versus reduced bucket, unique/multimap, tree-bin, ownership-link, and migration-state terminology.
Separated arithmetic average chain length from probability-model expectations and worst-case maximum chain length.
notation_and_syntax.notes: Reduction is always scoped to positive m; lazy zero-bucket state branches before modulo.

evidence: Replayed identity hashes 0,5,10,2 into five buckets and confirmed lengths 3,0,1,0,0 and maximum three.
Confirmed updating key 5 preserves size four and yields FIVE.
Recomputed placement under eleven buckets as four singleton chains, then deletion of 10 yields keys 0,2,5 and size three.
Checked n=120,m=100 gives valid chaining load alpha=1.2.
numerical_recomputation.notes: Python integer hashing matches the fixture values used; the trace does not generalize to arbitrary key hashes.

evidence: Verified sum Li=n and arithmetic mean alpha=n/m.
Derived expected unsuccessful candidate count alpha only under uniform/independent query-bucket assumptions.
Reviewed lookup completeness and equality confirmation from the exact-bucket invariant.
Reviewed stop-the-world and incremental rehash as one-to-one placement transformations over live entries.
symbolic_recomputation.notes: Successful constants, tails, and per-operation bounds are not claimed without insertion/query/independence premises.

evidence: Reviewed m=0/1, empty/singleton, duplicate update/reject/multimap, head/middle/tail deletion, clear, cached hash, checked growth, allocation/callback failure, and destructor reentrancy.
Reviewed alpha below/equal/above thresholds, constant hash, Lmax=n, expensive equality/key hashing, treeification ordering, reference/iterator invalidation, and serialization order.
Reviewed two-table new/old authority, partially migrated buckets, duplicate prevention, one-huge-bucket budget failure, grow/shrink, seed change, pause/snapshot iteration, and completion.
Reviewed single/striped/bucket locking, resize coordination, atomic publication, stale readers, reclamation, and HashDoS/resource limits.
boundary_and_adversarial_cases.notes: A constant hash is required as a semantic stress case even though performance intentionally degrades.

evidence: Checked every executable entry appears once in the bucket selected by its current key and bucket count.
Checked stored keys are unique, counted size equals enumerated entries, update changes no membership, and delete changes exactly one membership.
Reviewed link/root, bucket length, cached hash, allocator ownership, and old/new migration authority consistency.
invariant_checking.notes: The educational list buckets do not establish node-allocation, iterator stability, or concurrent lifetime safety.

evidence: Reviewed find/insert/update/delete abstraction preservation and commit points.
Reviewed link-to-current deletion for head and interior nodes and unlink-before-destroy ordering.
Reviewed full-hash redistribution rather than copying old bucket numbers.
Reviewed per-bucket incremental migration authority and exact-once physical/logical membership.
proof_review.notes: Tree-bin and concurrent-map correctness remain implementation-specific proof obligations.

evidence: Expected O(1)/alpha claims name their hash/query assumptions and preserve O(Lmax) worst case.
OpenJDK treeification and Redis incremental rehash are explicitly current implementation examples, not ADT requirements.
Hash randomization, tree bins, limits, telemetry, locking, and reclamation are presented as layered mechanisms rather than universal guarantees.
proof_sketch_labeling.notes: No bucket representation is inferred from the C++/Java map abstraction alone.

evidence: The standard-library Python trace passed exact nine-line stdout, empty stderr, and zero exit status under recorded Python 3.14.4.
It emits evidence=finite_separate_chaining_trace and is explicitly limited against allocator, pointer, concurrency, and production-performance claims.
All ten final source destinations and all repository-local links were checked directly.
empirical_evidence_labeling.notes: No linked-node allocator, OpenJDK/Redis implementation, failure injection, concurrent history, reclamation scheme, collision attack, tree-bin conversion, migration latency, or production benchmark was empirically evaluated.

conceptual_review.notes: Reviewed map/multimap semantics, bucket placement, lookup/update/delete, expected/worst cost, container layouts, load, stop-the-world/incremental rehash, iteration/order, HashDoS, concurrency, and evidence.

practitioner_review.notes: Reviewed lazy allocation, full-hash caching, allocation/callback transaction boundaries, node ownership, destructor order, thresholds/histograms, migration budgets/authority, grow/shrink, iterator/reference policy, serialization, locking/reclamation, input limits, telemetry, and realistic workload measurement.

pedagogical_review.notes: Builds collision handling from the map abstraction, keeps correctness independent of distribution, compares bucket and migration designs, scopes current production examples, provides a reproduced operation trace, twelve causal misconceptions, ten varied examples, and five progressive exercises with complete answers.

limitations: Internal authoring, source, mathematical, executable-snippet, conceptual, practitioner, and pedagogical evidence only; no external language/runtime, allocator, concurrency, security, database, Redis/OpenJDK/Linux/Abseil maintainer, reliability, operations, architecture, or independent academic review is claimed. The chapter and finite trace prove neither generic exception/lifetime safety, expected O(1) for arbitrary inputs, bounded collision chains, tree-bin correctness, HashDoS immunity, iterator/reference stability beyond a named implementation, incremental migration latency, thread safety, memory reclamation, benchmark superiority, certification, nor deployment fitness.
